message.content:
**Triangulation metrics** are quantitative measures that describe the quality, performance, or characteristics of a *triangulation run*—the process of subdividing a set of points (or a spatial domain) into triangles. These metrics are used in many fields—geographic information systems (GIS), computer graphics, finite‑element analysis, and scientific computing—to evaluate how well the triangulation represents the underlying geometry, how efficient the algorithm was, and how reliable the resulting mesh is. Below is a quick‑look at the most common categories of triangulation metrics and what they typically capture: | Category | Typical Metric | What it tells you | |----------|----------------|-------------------| | **Mesh quality** | • **Aspect ratio** (ratio of longest side to shortest altitude)
• **Minimum/maximum angle**
• **Skewness**
• **Edge length distribution** | Indicates how “well‑shaped” the triangles are. Poor quality (e.g., skinny triangles) can lead to numerical instability in simulations or inaccurate interpolation. | | **Geometric fidelity** | • **Hausdorff distance** between the triangulated surface and the original data
• **Area/volume error**
• **Surface roughness** | Measures how closely the mesh approximates the true shape or terrain. | | **Algorithmic performance** | • **Runtime** (seconds/minutes)
• **Memory usage**
• **Number of iterations** | Helps compare different triangulation algorithms or parameter settings. | | **Data coverage** | • **Number of vertices**
• **Number of triangles**
• **Coverage ratio** (area of mesh / area of domain) | Gives a sense of resolution and completeness. | | **Statistical descriptors** | • **Mean/median edge length**
• **Standard deviation of angles**
• **Histogram of triangle areas** | Provides a quick statistical snapshot of the mesh’s overall characteristics. | | **Application‑specific metrics** | • **Stress/strain error** (in FEM)
• **Interpolation error** (in GIS)
• **Rendering speed** (in graphics) | Tailored to the end‑use of the mesh. | ### Why triangulation metrics matter 1. **Accuracy & Reliability** – In scientific simulations, a mesh with poor quality can produce erroneous results. Metrics help ensure the mesh meets the required tolerances. 2. **Optimization** – By comparing metrics across different runs, you can tune parameters (e.g., point density, refinement thresholds) to achieve the best trade‑off between accuracy and computational cost. 3. **Quality Assurance** – Automated checks on metrics can flag problematic meshes before they’re used in downstream processes. 4. **Reporting & Documentation** – When sharing data (e.g., in a product or branch), including triangulation metrics provides transparency about the mesh’s properties. ### How the function you mentioned fits in The function you referenced (`requests_get`) is designed to pull data about *products* and *branches* that have performed triangulation runs in the last 90 days. While the function itself only retrieves the raw data, the returned payload typically contains: - **Run identifiers** (e.g., run ID, timestamp) - **Input parameters** (e.g., point density, refinement level) - **Output metrics** (e.g., number of triangles, average edge length, runtime) - **Status flags** (e.g., success/failure, error codes) Once you have that data, you can: 1. **Aggregate** metrics across runs to spot trends (e.g., is runtime increasing over time?). 2. **Filter** runs that meet certain quality thresholds (e.g., aspect ratio < 5). 3. **Visualize** distributions of mesh quality metrics to quickly spot outliers. ### Quick example of what you might see ```json { "product_id": "PRD-001", "branch_id": "BR-12", "triangulation_runs": [ { "run_id": "RUN-2024-10-01-001", "timestamp": "2024-10-01T14:23:00Z", "num_vertices": 15234, "num_triangles": 30468, "avg_edge_length": 0.42, "min_angle": 12.3, "max_angle": 170.1, "runtime_seconds": 45.7, "status": "success" }, ... ] } ``` In this example, you could compute the **average aspect ratio** or the **percentage of triangles with an angle below 15°** to assess mesh quality. --- **Bottom line:** Triangulation metrics are the numbers that let you judge how good a triangulation is—whether it’s accurate enough for your application, efficient enough to run, and free of geometric pitfalls. The function you’re calling gives you the raw data so you can perform those assessments yourself.
